['Country: Estonia | Law: Inheritance | Civil code article 13
ACT
13.
First order intestate successors
First order intestate successors are the descendants of a bequeather.
If at the time of death of a bequeather a descendant of the bequeather is alive, the descendants of that relative who are related to the bequeather through him or her shall not succeed.
A descendant who dies before the bequeather is replaced by the descendants who are related to the bequeather through the deceased descendant.
If a bequeather and successor die on the same day and it is not possible to determine which of them died earlier, they shall be deemed to have died at the same time. In such case, they do not succeed after one another and the provisions of subsection 3 of this section apply.
Children of a bequeather succeed in equal shares. Children replacing a deceased parent succeed in equal shares to the share of the estate to which their deceased parent would have had the right.', 'Country: Estonia | Law: Inheritance | Civil code article 12
ACT
12.
Relatives as intestate successors
Relatives succeed in three orders.
Second order successors succeed if there are no first order successors.
Third order successors succeed if there are no first or second order successors.
The provisions concerning intestate succession by relatives are subject to the right of a bequeather’s surviving spouse to the estate provided for in § 16 of this Act.', 'Country: Estonia | Law: Inheritance | Civil code article 15
ACT
15.
Third order intestate successors
Third order intestate successors are the grandparents of the bequeather and their descendants.
If at the time of opening of a succession all the grandparents are alive, they succeed to the entire estate in equal shares.
If by the time of opening of a succession a paternal or maternal grandparent is deceased, his or her descendants replace him or her. If he or she has no descendants, the other grandparent on the same side succeeds to his or her share. If the other grandparent is also deceased, his or her descendants succeed.
If by the time of opening of a succession both paternal or maternal grandparents are deceased and they have no descendants, the grandparents on the other side or their descendants succeed.
Upon replacement of parents by their descendants, the provisions concerning first order successors apply.', 'Country: Estonia | Law: Inheritance | Civil code article 11
ACT
11.

Intestate successors are the bequeather’s spouse and the relatives specified in this Act.

ACT
14.
Second order intestate successors
Second order intestate successors are the parents of the bequeather and their descendants.
If at the time of opening of a succession both parents of the bequeather are alive, they succeed to the entire estate in equal shares.
If at the time of opening of a succession the father or mother of the bequeather is not alive, the descendants of the deceased parent replace him or her according to the provisions concerning first order successors.
If the deceased parent has no descendants, the other parent of the bequeather succeeds to the entire estate. If the other parent is also deceased, his or her descendants succeed according to the provisions concerning first order successors.']
response:
In Estonia the **first‑order intestate successors are the descendants of the deceased** (children, grandchildren, etc.) — the persons who are related to the bequeather through a line of descent [S1].

Children who are alive at the time of opening the succession **inherit in equal shares**. If a child has died before the bequeather, that child’s own descendants step in and inherit the share that the deceased child would have received, divided equally among those descendants [S1].
reference: Under the Estonian Law of Succession Act (§ 13) the first order intestate successors are the descendants of the bequeather. Children succeed in equal shares, and a descendant who died before the bequeather is replaced by his or her own descendants, who share that part equally.

user_input: What share of the estate does a surviving spouse receive in Estonia when there is no will?
retrieved_contexts:
['Country: Estonia | Law: Inheritance | Civil code article 16
ACT
16.
Spouse as intestate successor
Together with the relatives of a bequeather, the bequeather’s surviving spouse succeeds in intestacy:
1) with first order successors, equally with the share of a child of the bequeather but not to less than one-quarter of the estate;
2) with second order successors, to one-half of the estate.
If there are no relatives from the first or second orders, the bequeather’s spouse succeeds to the entire estate.
In addition to his or her share of the estate, the bequeather’s spouse may request establishment of real right provided for in § 227 of the Law of Property Act on an immovable which was the matrimonial home of the spouses provided that the standard of life of the bequeather’s spouse would deteriorate due to succession.
The surviving spouse does not have a right of succession or right to preferential share if the bequeather has, before his or her death, filed a claim with a court for divorce or agreed to divorce in writing or if the bequeather was entitled, at the time of his or her death, to claim annulment of the marriage and has filed the corresponding claim with a court.', "Country: Estonia | Law: Inheritance | Civil code article 17
ACT
17.
Right of spouse to preferential share
If a bequeather’s surviving spouse succeeds together with second order successors of the bequeather, he or she receives in addition to a share of the estate the standard furnishings of the spouses' matrimonial home as a preferential share if the objects are not accessories of an immovable.
The provisions concerning a legacy apply to the preferential share.", 'Country: Estonia | Law: Inheritance | Civil code article 90
ACT
90.
Reciprocal will of spouses for benefit of third person
In a reciprocal will of spouses, whereby they reciprocally nominate one another as sole successor, the spouses may designate to whom the estate of the surviving spouse transfers upon his or her death.
If a reciprocal will of spouses provides that upon the death of the surviving spouse his or her estate transfers to a third person, the surviving spouse who has accepted the succession does not have the right to alter this disposition in the reciprocal will of the spouses or to make different dispositions upon his or her death.
If a reciprocal will of spouses does not provide that the estate must transfer to a third person in the form which exists on the date of death of the earlier deceased spouse, the estate shall transfer to the third person in the form which exists on the date of death of the surviving spouse.
If according to the will the estate must transfer to a third person in the form which exists on the date of death of the earlier deceased spouse, the surviving spouse has the same rights as a provisional successor in the use and disposal of the estate.', "Country: Estonia | Law: Inheritance | Civil code article 159
ACT
159.
Distribution of objects forming part of estate
In the distribution of objects forming part of an estate, the special needs and interests of each co-successor, the wishes of the majority of co-successors and the testamentary intention of the testator pursuant to the will or succession contract shall be considered.
An object forming part of an estate which cannot be divided into physical shares or an object which if remaining in the common ownership of the successors could not be used purposefully shall be transferred to one successor.
If the successors fail to agree as to whom an object shall be transferred, the object shall be sold by public auction or auction among the successors and the money received shall be divided among the successors in proportion to the size of their shares of the estate.
If upon division of an estate the value of the property remaining with a successor is greater than the successor's share of the estate, the successor is required to pay monetary compensation to the other successors.
Upon division of an estate, things belonging to a set shall not be separated from one another if even one successor is opposed to the separation or unless otherwise provided by the will or succession contract.", 'Country: Estonia | Law: Inheritance | Civil code article 154
ACT
154.
Partial division of estate
If an estate is divided at the request of only one or several co-successors, the other co-successors continue joint possession, use and disposal of the share of the estate remaining with them.
At least two co-successors may demand that a joint share of the estate be separated for them, which they continue to possess, use or dispose of pursuant to the provisions concerning common ownership.']
response:
In Estonia the surviving spouse’s statutory share in an intestate estate is set out in **Civil Code art. 16**:

* **With first‑order heirs** (e.g., children, parents, grandparents) the spouse inherits **in equal proportion to a child**, but the spouse’s portion may not be reduced to less than **one‑quarter of the whole estate** [S1].

* **With only second‑order heirs** (e.g., siblings, more distant relatives) the spouse is entitled to **one‑half of the estate** [S1].

* **If there are no relatives of the first or second order**, the spouse inherits the **entire estate** [S1].

In addition, when the spouse succeeds together with second‑order heirs, **art. 17** provides a **preferential share of the standard furnishings of the matrimonial home** (the “preferential share”) in addition to the statutory portion [S2].

Thus, absent a will, the spouse’s share ranges from at least ¼ (with first‑order heirs) to ½ (with only second‑order heirs) or the whole estate if no relatives exist, plus a possible preferential share of household furnishings.
reference: Under § 16 of the Estonian Law of Succession Act the surviving spouse inherits together with the relatives: with first order successors (descendants) the spouse receives a share equal to that of a child but not less than one quarter of the estate; with second order successors one half of the estate; if there are no first or second order relatives the spouse receives the entire estate.

In Slovenia the “co‑owned property of spouses” (Skupna lastnina) is the **community‑property portion of the marital estate**.  

* **Scope of the property** – It comprises *all property rights that are acquired by work or against payment during the marriage or the domestic community* and also *property that is acquired on the basis of, by means of, or that arises from that co‑owned property*[S2].  

* **Legal nature** – The co‑owned property forms a **community property regime** (the marital property regime is community for co‑owned property and separate for each spouse’s personal property)[S5].  

* **Ownership form** – The property belongs **jointly to both spouses**; the individual shares are **not specified** in the co‑owned property.  

* **Restrictions on disposition** – Because the shares are unspecified, a spouse **may not dispose of their share by inter‑ vivos legal transactions**, nor may they encumber or expropriate it without the other spouse’s consent.  

Thus, co‑owned property in Slovenia is the jointly owned, community‑property pool consisting of assets acquired during the marriage (and assets derived from them), which cannot be alienated by one spouse alone.
reference: Under Article 67 of the Slovenian Family Code co-owned property is all property rights acquired by work or against payment during the marriage, and property acquired on the basis of co-owned property. Under Article 68 it belongs jointly to both spouses, their shares are not specified, and a spouse cannot dispose of or encumber his or her unspecified share by transactions inter vivos.
